items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: Frank Sinatra, Bing Crosby, Ella Fitzgerald, they’ve all said there was nobody like Armstrong and they all copied and learned from him.

ctx.x: Yeah if you listen to “West End Blues” I think that’s all you need to hear to back up that statement.

Yup. And it’s interesting on “West End Blues” he uses that wordless vocal in the latter part of the recording, which is perfectly in keeping with what he has played. I love that record as an example of Armstrong as the complete lyric performer and the great technician as well. The fact that he sings a vocal that has no words is completely fitting to that aspect of his work, because the words don’t make any difference and he treats the words like that in many of his vocal performances. And yet when he wants to…
Do you suppose that performance, and especially that introduction was completely spontaneous?

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Except for Bing Crosby... I used to listen to it. Just before him came a 15-minute program... I knew who he was and I liked the pop songs of the time

ctx.x: The thing that I think will surprise people who are younger than we, is that you are talking about pop music, and that’s what jazz was.

Yes, it was. There was no separate category anywhere in the press and so on. There was almost no press, in fact. Down Beat was operating at the time. So was Metronome, which was an older magazine. But you had no things – no references to jazz or even really to pop music as a separate category in the ordinary day-to-day press. This really started to break open through Benny Goodman, because he became so popular so quickly. He was sort of a special phenomenon. People did not write articles about Bing Crosby, for…

Mann School for Boys. It’s just a mile-and-a-half away from here. I never thought I’d live up here, near the school, but I became very found of Riverdale when I went to Horace Mann. The way that came about was that – of course I had gotten quite a few Ellington – well, I started to think about how the Ellington band grew out of – in my consciousness – out of my interest in Casa Loma and Benny Goodman and Fletcher Henderson. But that’s something we’ll come back to later. The interview with Goodman came about,…
